To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the fractional contribution to the acetyl CoA pool of 13C labeled octanoate in the intact rat is highest in heart and sole muscle followed by red and white portions of gastrocnemus muscle and then liver.

the fractional contribution to oxidative metabolism correlates to oxidative capacity of the muscle and that contraction increases the rate of octanoate metabolism in proportion to the increase in oxidative rate.

the fractional contribution to acetyl-CoA of octanoate oxidation correlates with the oxidative capacity of a tissue and that octanoyl oxidation in contracting muscle is increased in proportion to overall increases in oxidative metabolism.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a non-invasive, nonradioactive, in vivo technique for measuring fatty acid oxidation.
the development of a new method for the measurement of fatty acid oxidation in vivo.
the study of the metabolism of fatty acids, particularly the medium-chain fatty acid octanoate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the oxidation of fatty acids, including octanoate, is highest in tissues with high oxidative capacities and that the oxidation of octanoate increases in contracting muscle in proportion to increases in oxidative rate.
the fractional contribution to acetyl-CoA is highest in heart and soleous muscle and lowest in liver and WG.
the fractional contribution to oxidative metabolism of octanoate is highest in heart and skeletal muscle followed by liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oxidative capacity of a tissue is directly proportional to its fractional contribution of octanate to oxidative metabolism.
13C-NMRS is an effective technique to assess fatty acid oxidation and that octanoic acid is an effective tracer for the study of fatty acid oxidation in the intact animal.
octanoate is oxidized to the acetyl CoA pool in all the tissues studied and that this oxidation is highest in the heart and skeletal muscles with the highest oxidative capacity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
octanoate is a major contributor to acetyl-CoA in all of these tissues, and it is the predominant substrate in the heart and soleus.
octanoate oxidation is a major contributor to the oxidative metabolism in all tissues examined.
octanoate is a major fuel for oxidative metabolism in heart, liver and skeletal muscle.
